analysis.one_liner: Requires large banks to stop financing new fossil fuel projects and cut financed emissions.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the House Financial Services Committee; it died at the end of the 118th Congress without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The Fossil Free Financing Act would have required banks with at least $50 billion in assets to file plans with the Federal Reserve to eliminate financed emissions — the pollution their lending and investments cause. It would have banned bank financing of new or expanded fossil fuel projects immediately, thermal coal by 2025, and all fossil fuel financing by 2030, with penalties including forced divestment and potential loss of FDIC insurance for banks that don't comply. Plans could not rely on carbon offsets, and banks would have to prioritize lending for worker severance and retraining in affected communities.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who face the health and economic costs of climate change — particularly low-income and minority communities that the bill says banks must prioritize when withdrawing funding from polluting projects — plus workers who would receive severance and retraining financing, and anyone whose money is in banks exposed to fossil fuel-related financial risk.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities hit by climate change and pollution

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits bank financing of new or expanded fossil fuel projects immediately, thermal coal by 2025, and all fossil fuel financing by 2030.

Requires banks to reach plans that cut financed emissions 50% by 2030 and zero by 2050, aligned with the 1.5°C science-based target, and bars them from using carbon offsets to paper over the difference.

Requires banks to prioritize withdrawing funding from projects that disproportionately harm low-income and minority communities, and to finance severance and retraining for workers affected by the transition.
Adds banks' contribution to financed emissions as a factor in Financial Stability Oversight Council supervision, treating climate-driven lending as a financial stability risk.
Gives the Federal Reserve real enforcement tools: penalties, required divestiture of assets, and possible termination of FDIC insurance for a noncompliant bank's depository institution.

analysis.who_pays: Large banks ($50 billion-plus in assets) that currently earn fees and interest from oil, gas, and coal lending, underwriting, and deal-making, and fossil fuel companies that would lose access to big-bank financing. Some of that cost could be passed to borrowers through reduced credit availability for energy projects.
analysis.who_pays_short: Big banks and fossil fuel companies

drawbacks.text: The immediate ban on financing new or expanded fossil fuel projects, without a parallel federal plan to replace the energy supply, could raise energy costs or constrain supply in the short run, hitting household energy bills.

The bill applies its strictest mandate to banks with $50 billion or more in assets, so fossil financing could migrate to smaller lenders or foreign banks not covered by US law, reducing its environmental effect while still disadvantaging US banks.

Opponents in the financial and energy industries would argue that mandating portfolio choices through bank regulation turns the Federal Reserve into an instrument of industrial policy and could increase financial stability risk by forcing rapid divestment at once.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would impose a large, binding constraint on the main channel through which money funds fossil fuel expansion, with strong enforcement and explicit worker and community protections. Its main weaknesses are the absence of any accompanying plan for energy supply or prices during the transition, and the possibility that financing shifts to institutions the bill does not cover. On its own terms it is well designed; it is also very unlikely to become law in any Congress where a majority of either chamber opposes mandatory fossil fuel financing limits.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in March 2023 and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2025 without ever reaching a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Ayanna Pressley introduced the Fossil Free Financing Act of 2023 on March 30, 2023, with Reps. Tlaib, Jayapal, and Bowman as original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the day it was introduced, and no further action was ever recorded.
It attracted 21 cosponsors, all Democrats, and never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or action in the Senate.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large banks and fossil fuel companies are better off: they kept unrestricted access to big-bank financing for new and expanded fossil fuel projects, and the Federal Reserve never had to treat financed emissions as a supervisory matter. Households and communities exposed to climate and financial risk gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big banks and fossil fuel companies

sides.party_line_note: All 21 cosponsors were Democrats and the sponsor is a progressive Democrat; with Republicans holding the House majority, the bill had no path to a vote.

industries.note: These banks — the JPMorgans, Citis, and Bank of Americas of the financial system — would have been forced to file and meet emission reduction plans, barred from new fossil fuel financing, and faced Fed penalties, forced divestiture, and possible loss of FDIC insurance for noncompliance. Their interest in killing the bill ran against ordinary people's exposure to climate and financial risk.

Fossil fuel companies and projects deriving 15% or more of revenue from oil, gas, or coal would have lost access to new big-bank financing immediately, and all financing by 2030, raising their cost of capital and stalling new projects.
The bill explicitly prohibits plans from relying on carbon offsets, cutting off a market banks and emitters use to claim emissions reductions without actual cuts.

industries.industry: Credit rating and asset management firms supervising nonbank financial companies
industries.note: Nonbank financial companies supervised by the Fed would have had financed emissions added to the factors considered in designating and supervising them, adding compliance burden and potential constraints.
